newsitem.title: GERMANY: UNILEVER SHRUGS OFF GREENPEACE SOYA PROTEST.
newsitem.headline: UNILEVER SHRUGS OFF GREENPEACE SOYA PROTEST.

text.p: The German headquarters of Anglo-Dutch consumer products group Unilever shrugged off noisy protests against the planned use of genetically-altered soy products outside its main building on Thursday.
Some 40 activists from environmentalist group Greenpeace, dressed as rabbits, played loud music and displayed banners saying "No to gene-altered soya in our food products."
"They are asking us to oppose the new products, which we won't do," said a Unilever spokesman.
"If we did this because of consumer concerns, it would seriously disturb the raw materials markets and the consumers would have to pay the bill in the end."
"We have a positive attitude towards biotechnology."
The activists said their outfits were aimed at demonstrating what they saw as the planned role of humans as laboratory animals testing the new products.
They will be derived from genetically-modified U.S. soybeans, which have been adapted for tolerance to a weed-killer, and are cleared by European Union health authorities for import from late 1996.
Greenpeace says dangers to human health and the environment cannot be excluded.
The campaign, started in September, has contributed to a premium of rape oil over soy oil in Rotterdam, as traders favoured rape products to avoid any impact from the political row.
This morning, Nov/Jan rape oil was at 98.00 guilders per 100 kilos fob mill compared with soy oil at 93.50.
Traders said the anti-soya campaign was restricted to Germany as it not had not caught on elsewhere.
They believed it could end soon if crushers and large food companies defused it.
Soya is used in some 30,000 individual food products here.
Screening and labelling of products derived from modified and unmodified beans -- one of the consumer lobby's demands -- would inevitably result in additional costs.
